Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology of back pain in children.
Assess the potential etiologies of back pain in children.
Discuss the various classification systems for spondylolisthesis.
Identify important red flags for more serious causes of back pain in children found during the
patient history and physical examination.
Determine the indications for various imaging modalities in children with back pain.
Outline the various treatment options for mechanical back pain, spondylolysis, and
spondylolisthesis.

Back pain in children is common. More than 50% of children experience back pain by age 15
years.1
The incidence of spondylolysis is 5%, and it occurs in males more often than females. The
incidence is 53% in Inuits. Of patients with spondylolysis, 25% have associated
spondylolisthesis.
Of patients with isthmic spondylolisthesis, males are affected more commonly than females,
but high-grade spondylolisthesis is four times more likely in females than males.
Spondylolisthesis primarily affects L5 (in 87% to 95% of patients); less frequently L4 (=10%) and
L3 (=3%).
Etiology
In as many as 80% of children with back pain, no identifying cause is found. Miller et al2
evaluated 2,846 children (mean age, 14 years) with back pain and reported that 2,159 (76%) of
the children had no underlying etiology for the back pain.
Watch the following video (2:00–5:05 min) by Herman3 on idiopathic back pain in children,
which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland Resident Webinar Series.
Heavy backpacks are associated with a higher incidence of back pain. Specifically, Chen and
Mu4 found that a child’s backpack weighing more than or equal to 15% of the child’s body
weight may create increased forces that may contribute to back pain.
In evaluating a new patient for back pain, three potential etiologies should be considered.
Mechanical back pain with no underlying cause
Back pain secondary to spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis
Back pain secondary to a more serious cause that may require extensive workup
Older children and adolescents commonly experience adult-like low back pain (i.e., pain with
no clear etiology and related to deconditioning or strain of the paraspinal muscles).
Often, in children younger than 10 years, no underlying cause is found, but the following
serious underlying pathology should be considered.
Intra-abdominal pathology, such as pyelonephritis, pancreatitis, and appendicitis
Neoplasms of the spinal column
The most common malignant cause of back pain in children is leukemia.
Traumatic fractures of the spine
Apophyseal ring fractures occur at the junction of the vertebral body and the cartilaginous
ring apophysis, with the posteroinferior portion displaced into the canal.

Spinal cord anomalies, such as tethered cord
Osteomyelitis and/or diskitis
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis5 (Resource 1)
Often a diagnosis of exclusion
The increased prevalence of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis among athletes suggests that
increased mechanical stresses across the lumbar spine may be an important factor. For
example, the incidence of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis ranges from 15% to 50% in
college football players and is as high as 11% in children who participate in gymnastics.6,7
Watch the following video (3:50–7:23 min) by Beasley et al8 on the diagnosis, management,
and return to sport associated with spondylolysis..
Anatomy and Classification
Watch the following video (2:14–4:09 min) by Oetgen9 on spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis,
which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland Resident Webinar Series.
It is important to understand the anatomy of the lumbar spine and the overall sagittal
alignment that contributes to spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis. The alignment of the
lumbar spine and, therefore, the mechanical stresses at the lumbosacral junction, are altered
by the morphology of the sacrum and pelvis.
Pelvic incidence is a parameter that is individual to each person; it includes sacral slope and
pelvic tilt (Figure 1; Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:35 PM
AAOS | Pediatric and Adolescent Back Pain: Pediatric Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000582

Figure 1 Illustration shows pelvic incidence, which is comprised of the sacral slope and pelvic
tilt. (Reproduced from Hu SS, Wood KB: Sagittal imbalance of the spine, in Truumees E, Prather
H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 357-369.)
Patients with an abnormal pelvic incidence appear to be predisposed to spondylolysis and
spondylolisthesis. For example, patients with a high pelvic incidence and sacral slope appear to
have increased shear stresses at the L5-S1 disk, which increases the loading forces observed at
the L5 pars interarticularis. Conversely, patients with a low pelvic incidence may experience
increased impingement of the L5 pars with the facets of L4 during back extension.10
No formal classification system exists for mechanical back pain; however, it routinely is divided
into acute and chronic back pain. At least three major classification systems are used to
categorize the type and severity of spondylolisthesis, which may cause back pain in children.
Watch Video 1 (1:04-1:22 min) by Faldini et al on the reduction of unbalanced severe isthmic
spondylolisthesis. (Video 1).

Meyerding classification system is used to quantify the degree of spondylolisthesis Grade I is
a slippage of zero to 25%
grade II is a slippage of 26% to 50%
grade III is a slippage of 51% to 75%,
grade IV is a slippage of 76% to 99%
Grade V in this classification system is spondyloptosis, or more than 100% anterior
translation of the superior vertebra over the inferior vertebra (Figure 2; Resource 3).

Figure 2 Illustrations show the Meyerding classification of spondylolisthesis. The numbers
1 through 4 in each image denote the fraction of the slip anteriorly. For example, 1 equals
one-fourth (25%). A, Normal vertebral alignment. B, Grade I, zero to 25% translation. C,
Grade II, 26% to 50% translation. D, Grade III, 51% to 75% translation. E, Grade IV, 76% to
100% translation. F, Grade V, spondyloptosis. (Reproduced from Khalil JG, Fischgrund JS,
Roberts RV: Lumbar stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis, in Truumees E, Prather H,
eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 253-264.)
Wiltse classification system
The Wiltse classification divides spondylolisthesis into five major types (and several
subtypes) based on radiologic findings (Figure 3; Resource 4).
Dysplastic: Congenital defect of the lumbosacral facet joints; the translation is secondary
to an abnormal neural arch formation in utero.
Isthmic: The lumbosacral facets are nonpathologic, but the spondylolisthesis is caused by
a defect in the pars interarticularis. This subtype can be further divided depending on
whether the pars fracture is lytic, elongated, or acute.

Degenerative: Secondary to arthritic breakdown of the facet joints with associated
intersegmental instability
Traumatic: Occurs secondary to an acute fracture of the pars interarticularis
Pathologic: Associated with diffuse or local disease that compromises the usual structural
integrity that prevents slippage
Figure 3 Illustration shows the Wiltse classification of spondylolisthesis. A, Normal. B, Type
1, dysplastic. C, Type IIA, break in the pars interarticularis. D, Type IIB, elongated but intact
pars interarticularis. E, Type IIC, acute fracture. F, Type III, degenerative. G, Type IV, fracture
other than that of the pars interarticularis. H, Type V, pathologic. (Reproduced from Parent
S, Labelle H, Mac-Thiong JM: Spondylolisthesis in children and young adults, in Truumees E,
Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 371-380.)
Spinal Deformity Study Group classification system

This classification system considers the pelvic incidence, grade of the slippage, overall
spinopelvic balance, and lumbosacral kyphosis (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Algorithm shows the Spinal Deformity Study Group classification of
spondylolisthesis. Types 1 through 3 are low-grade spondylolisthesis, and types 4 through 6
are high-grade spondylolisthesis. Four important characteristics can be measured on
sagittal radiographs: slip, pelvic incidence (PI), spinopelvic balance, and lumbosacral
kyphosis (LSK). (Reproduced from Parent S, Labelle H, Mac-Thiong JM: Spondylolisthesis in
children and young adults, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 371-380.)
Patient History and Physical Examination Findings
Patient History
Watch the following video (7:24–8:20 min) by Beasley et al8 on the diagnosis, management,
and return to sport associated with spondylolysis.
It is important to be systematic in discussing the back pain present in a child. It often is helpful
to have the child point with a finger to the exact location of the back pain. Then the clinician
can proceed with follow-up questions.
SEND FEEDBACK

How long has the back pain been present? Days, months, or years?
Does the pain stay in your back or does it shoot down your legs?
If you had to rate your pain on a scale of 10, with 10 being the worst pain in your life (as if a
dog were biting you), how would you currently rate your pain right?
Do you play any sports? If so, which ones?
Pay attention to sports that involve back extension movements, such as gymnastics, diving,
and dancing. Weightlifting also is associated with back pain and disk disease.
Does your pain ever wake you up from your sleep?
Pain at night traditionally is associated with tumors.
Are you wetting the bed or urinating frequently or urgently?
Have you taken anything, such as NSAIDs, for the pain? Have you undergone any physical
therapy to help the pain?
Visceral pain is not relieved by rest or exacerbated by activity.
Do you have any family history of degenerative disk disease?
Watch the following video (1:20–3:11) by Gresh11 on physical examination and imaging of
pediatric back pain, which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland Resident
Webinar Series.
Physical Examination
The physical examination should begin with a visual inspection of the child posteriorly and
anteriorly. Evaluate for the presence of hairy patches on the skin. Particular attention should
be paid to substantial sagittal or coronal malalignment, which indicates underlying scoliosis or
Scheuermann kyphosis.
Next, the back should be palpated in the midline and along the paraspinal muscles.
Range of motion of the back should be observed by asking the patient to perform a forward
bend test and to extend the back maximally.
The presence of severe back pain during extension suggests spondylolysis or
spondylolisthesis.
Watch the following video (8:21–10:05 min) by Beasley et al8 on the diagnosis, management,
and return to sport associated with spondylolysis.
Watch the following video (3:11–4:40 min) by Gresh11 on the physical examination and
imaging of pediatric back pain, which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland
Resident Webinar Series.
SEND FEEDBACK

A detailed musculoskeletal, abdominal, and neurologic examination is necessary (Video 2).
Video 2 Brooks JT: Video. Pediatric Spine Physical Examination. Jackson, MS, 2021.
During the pediatric neurologic examination, ask the child to walk on tip toes, heels, walk in a
straight line as if on a tight rope, hop on one leg, and perform a deep-knee squat. If a true
neurologic abnormality is present, the patient would unlikely be able to perform these
movements.
If an abnormality is detected on physical examination, a more focused examination should
include assessment of the reflexes of the upper and lower extremities (Table 1; Resources 5
and 6).

With the patient supine on the examination table, a straight leg test should be performed
to evaluate for radicular pain. The popliteal angle should be assessed to evaluate for

Symmetric sensation in the dermatomal distribution should be assessed.
A thorough neurologic examination also includes evaluating for clonus and upgoing toes on
the Babinski test.
Severe spondylolisthesis (Wiltse grade IV and grade V) eventually may result in gait
abnormalities in combination with a flexed hip and knee position when standing at
rest12 (Figure 5; Resource 7).

In addition to the strength of the bilateral upper and lower extremities and the sensation in
the dermatomal distribution, the following specific examination finding may help localize
the source of the pain.
The seated slump test puts maximal tension on the L5 and S1 nerve most often affected
by isthmic spondylolisthesis at L5-S1. The patient is asked to slump forward as the

Figure 6 Clinical photograph shows the seated slump test. To maximize tension on the L5
and S1 nerve roots, the seated patient is asked to slump forward. The symptomatic lower

Physical examination findings may include paraspinal muscle spasms, tight hamstrings, and
limited lumbar mobility.
High-grade spondylolisthesis can produce a waddling gait (Phalen-Dickson syndrome) and
hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine.
The nerve root most commonly affected by an isthmic spondylolisthesis at L5-S1 is L5
because of foraminal stenosis caused by fracture callus or inflammatory mediators of the
fracture released near the nerve root.
Popliteal angle measurements quantify the degree of hamstring tightness.

Imaging Studies
Watch the following video (10:12–19:40) by Beasley et al8 on the diagnosis, management, and
return to sport associated with spondylolysis.
Watch the following video (7:48–9:30 min) by Oetgen9 on spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis,
which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland Resident Webinar Series .
Radiography
Plain radiographs should be obtained first, typically standing PA and lateral views of the
lumbar spine.
Oblique radiographs traditionally have been used (to assess for the Scotty dog sign) but do not
substantially improve the sensitivity of the diagnosis and add considerable radiation exposure
and cost. Therefore, they are not recommended.
Computed Tomography
Watch the following video (4:40–7:25) by Gresh11 on physical examination and imaging of
pediatric back pain, which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland Resident Webinar
Series.
CT is best for identifying bone-related abnormalities (spondylolysis, apophyseal ring fracture)
and bone-producing neoplasms (osteoid osteoma).
CT is the best option for visualizing a pars defect; however, radiation exposure must be
considered.
In high-grade vertebral slips with substantial angulation of the cephalad vertebra, a Napoleon
hat sign may be observed on AP views (Figure 7).

Figure 7 AP pelvis radiograph (A) demonstrates an inverted Napoleon hat sign (arrows),

(Reproduced with permission from Pendergrast TE, Dyer RB: The “inverted Napoleon's hat”

Single-photon emission CT is highly sensitive for pars defects; however, radiation exposure is
high, and this type of CT rarely affects management. Therefore, this imaging modality is not
recommended for routine use.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is recommended for patients with any neurologic signs or symptoms. MRI has been
shown to be a sensitive initial advanced imaging modality for identifying structural causes of
back pain if concerning findings are present on patient history or physical examination.
MRI is associated with the advantage of avoiding the radiation exposure associated with CT or
bone scintigraphy.
MRI is suboptimal for evaluating pars defects and osteoid osteoma but has a role in assessing
nerve entrapment and/or the acuity of the pars injury.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
If a child presents with back pain that, based on the history and physical examination, appears
to be mechanical in etiology with no clear evidence of spondylolysis, standard treatment

AAOS | Pediatric and Adolescent Back Pain: Pediatric Spine

16/25

includes the following measures.
Cessation of sports activity, particularly if the child participates in a sport with back extension
activities
Scheduled NSAIDs
Physical therapy
Physical therapy often is focused on core strengthening and stretching of the hamstrings.
Watch the following video (33:35–38:59) by Beasley et al8 on the diagnosis, management,
and return to sport associated with spondylolysis.
Home exercise programs for lumbar spine strengthening also are available13 (Resource 8).
No consensus exists on how long management should continue. Most surgeons recommend 6
weeks to 3 months.
Controversy exists regarding whether adjunctive treatment with the use of a brace is helpful
for spondylolysis that has been diagnosed or is strongly suspected. Bracing in combination
with rest and NSAIDs may improve much of the back pain children experience; however, no
definitive data are available to prove this assumption.
Watch the following video (19:43–25:23 min) by Beasley et al8 on the diagnosis,
management, and return to sport associated with spondylolysis.
Watch the following video (9:30–13:10 min) by Oetgen9 on spondylolysis and
spondylolisthesis, which was presented at the 2020 University of Maryland Resident Webinar
Series.
The same nonsurgical treatment is recommended for patients with back pain secondary to
low-grade spondylolisthesis.
If activity modification, NSAIDs, and physical therapy in combination with bracing fail, an
injection of the pars by interventional radiology or pain management may be considered.
Surgical Management
Surgical management is guided by the underlying etiology of the child’s back pain.
If the child has back pain secondary to lumbar disk herniation and if the pain is unresponsive
to nonsurgical management for a minimum of 6 weeks or if neurologic symptoms are
present, then surgical treatment may be indicated. Approximately one-fourth of patients
with a lumbar disk herniation also have evidence of an apophyseal ring fracture and more
frequently require surgical treatment.
Back pain secondary to an osteoid osteoma usually is managed via surgical excision.
Radiofrequency ablation is less commonly used in the spine because of the possibility of

17/25

neurologic damage from proximity to the radiofrequency ablation probe.
For a child who has spondylolysis without evidence of spondylolisthesis and in whom all
nonsurgical treatment options have failed, four potential spinal instrumentation
configurations have been described. All four techniques are associated with an 80% to 90%
rate of return to sports (Figure 8).
Scott wiring technique
For the Scott wiring technique, wires are placed around the transverse process on each
side of and through the spinous process to compress the pars interarticularis defect. The
Scott wiring technique is the least rigid of the four fixation methods yet still results in a
healing rate of almost 80%.
Buck screw technique (direct pars repair)
Direct intralaminar screw fixation of a pars defect, which was described by Buck,14 is a
minimally invasive, motion-preserving technique that results in good outcomes in 93% of
patients.
Morscher pedicle screw and hook technique
Pedicle screws and infralaminar hooks that are attached to a short rod allow for
compression and stabilization of a pars interarticularis defect. The pedicle screw and hook
technique are the most rigid of the four fixation methods.
U-rod technique
Similar to the pedicle screw and hook technique, except that compression is applied by the
U-rod abutting the inferior aspect of the L5 spinous process
Currently, the direct pars repair technique and the pedicle screw and hook technique are
used more commonly. If a gap of more than 5 mm is present at the pars defect, then direct
pars repair is contraindicated.

For most children with high-grade (grade III or higher) spondylolisthesis, surgical treatment is
indicated. If a child has low-grade spondylolisthesis that is symptomatic and nonsurgical
treatment has failed, surgical treatment is indicated.
Review the following video by Sucato15 on how to reduce high-grade spondylolisthesis,
which was presented at the 12th International Pediatric Orthopaedic Symposium.
Controversy exists regarding whether spondylolisthesis should be fused in situ or reduced
and then fused.
Low-grade spondylolisthesis usually can be managed via postural reduction and in situ
fusion. The need for decompression can be determined based on the patient’s symptoms
and physical examination findings, with additional information obtained from advanced
imaging studies (CT and/or MRI).10
Central canal stenosis and/or foraminal stenosis should be ruled out; if present, formal or
indirect decompression should be performed. In situ fusion can be achieved via a Wiltse
approach (if no formal central decompression is required) or via a central midline
approach.
Posterolateral fusion with the use of autologous iliac crest bone graft remains the
preferred procedure for in situ fusion. If feasible, spinal instrumentation reduces the
need for prolonged immobilization; however, the space available for bone grafting is
reduced.
The management of high-grade spondylolisthesis remains somewhat controversial.10
It is key to decompress the L5 nerve root and visualize it during reduction.
Reduction of the spondylolisthesis completely is not necessary. Increased reduction may
lead to an increased risk of L5 nerve root traction injury.
Multiple technical approaches can be used to reduce spondylolisthesis.
Well-balanced, high-grade spondylolysis can be managed via in situ fusion.
Unbalanced high-grade spondylolisthesis can be managed via postural reduction of the
slip and anterior support with the use of allograft or a cage.

Surgical Management
Some historical cohort studies reported high complication rates with attempted
reduction.16,17 In addition, excellent clinical outcomes at long-term follow-up of in situ

fusion recently have been reported.18 With advancements in neuromonitoring and
surgical instrumentation in combination with an understanding of normal and
pathologic sagittal balance, a subset of patients with high-grade spondylolisthesis
likely may benefit from reduction procedures.
A clear distinction must be made between well-balanced, high-grade spondylolisthesis
(type 4) and unbalanced, high-grade spondylolisthesis (type 5 or type 6). The balanced
type 4 spondylolisthesis may be fused in situ after postural reduction on the surgical
table with the addition of pedicle and iliac screws. The fusion can be strengthened by
a fibular strut graft and/or by intervertebral screws spanning the L5-S1 space from an
S1 posteriorly based starting point. In patients who have high-grade spondylolisthesis
and pelvic retroversion with or without sagittal spinal imbalance (type 5 or type 6),
normal sagittal balance cannot be restored without correcting the lumbosacral
kyphosis and decreasing pelvic tilt or retroversion. The most important technical
points are that the L5 nerve root should be decompressed widely and be well-
visualized before any attempted reduction and every effort should be made to correct
lumbosacral kyphosis to decrease tension on the nerves and facilitate reduction. A
sacral dome osteotomy may be required to aid in lumbosacral kyphosis reduction.
Complete reduction of the slip is not mandatory. To reduce the risk of pseudarthrosis,
anterior support, in the form of an interbody cage, often is used with posteriorly
based pedicle screws, with or without additional iliac fixation.
Spondyloptosis (complete slippage of L5 over S1) is the most severe type of
translational spine deformity, and severe neurologic symptoms usually develop.
Spondyloptosis is one of the most challenging surgical problems. Because the
slippage is complete, surgical reduction of L5 over S1 usually is not possible. Proposed
treatment options include in situ fusion versus complete L5 vertebrectomy and
reduction of L4 over S1, which is a high-risk procedure with substantial complication
risk. If sagittal balance is preserved (i.e., a balanced spine with minimal sagittal
imbalance), the safest treatment option likely is in situ fusion with a fibular graft
placed through the vertebral body of S1 into the inferior end plate of L5, with
supplemental pedicle screw instrumentation to L4 and iliac screw fixation.

Injury to the L5 nerve root is the most common neurologic complication in reducing and fusing
L5-S1 spondylolisthesis. Reduction of the spondylolisthesis of more than 50% places the L5
nerve root at greater risk of injury.
Cauda equina syndrome (rare) is most likely to occur in a type 1 (dysplastic/congenital) slip,
with the intact posterior neural arch trapping the sacral nerve roots against the
posterosuperior corner of the sacrum. It may occur without surgical management as the slip
progresses.
Pseudoarthrosis occurs in as many as 45% of high-grade fusions without implants and as
many as 30% of high-grade slips managed via posterior instrumentation but is rare in high-
grade slips managed via circumferential fusion.
